description: This figure is a single tabular image (rendered as text, no axes, no scale bar, no micrograph) with five columns headed "Alloys^a", "Targeted properties", "Developers", "Aimed applications" and "Year", listing six historical Fe-Mn-Al-C-type steel developments in chronological order. Reading the rows top to bottom: Fe-13Mn-1.2C (high toughness and excellent wear resistance; Hadfield [15]; mining industry, cement mixers, railway switches; 1882); Fe-(20-50)Mn-(3-12)Al (good ductility and corrosion resistance; Dean and Anderson [16]; electrical heating elements; 1943); Fe-34Mn-10Al-0.76C (good corrosion and oxidation resistance; Ham and Cairns [17]; replacement of Cr-Ni stainless steels; 1958); Fe-(25-30)Mn-(8-10)Al-1C (precipitation hardening and good oxidation resistance; Kayak [18]; springs, gears, landing gears; 1969); Fe-30Mn-5Al-0.3C-Nb (high strength and elongation at lower temperatures; Kim et al. [10]; cryogenic structures; 1985); and Fe-(18-28)Mn-(9-12)Al-(0.7-1.2)C (low weight, high crash worthiness; Frommeyer and Brüx [6]; automotive body frames; 2000). The table therefore demonstrates the historical arc of Fe-Mn-Al-C alloy design from wear-resistant Hadfield-type steel (1882) through Cr-Ni stainless-steel replacement attempts (1958) to modern low-density automotive grades (2000), the final row marking the shift to weight reduction and crash worthiness. All cells are legible; the only legend element is the superscript "a" on "Alloys", whose footnote text is absent from the image.

subfigures.description: One five-column table titled by its header row: Alloys^a, Targeted properties, Developers, Aimed applications, Year. Six data rows span 1882 to 2000, from Fe-13Mn-1.2C (Hadfield [15]) to Fe-(18-28)Mn-(9-12)Al-(0.7-1.2)C (Frommeyer and Brüx [6]). All cells fully legible; no images, plots or scale bars.

observations.observation: The figure consists solely of a five-column table with the column headers 'Alloys^a', 'Targeted properties', 'Developers', 'Aimed applications' and 'Year'; it contains no micrographs, curves or spectra.
The table lists six alloys in ascending date order, spanning 1882 (Fe-13Mn-1.2C, Hadfield [15]) to 2000 (Fe-(18-28)Mn-(9-12)Al-(0.7-1.2)C, Frommeyer and Brüx [6]).

Row 1: Fe-13Mn-1.2C is listed with targeted properties 'High toughness and excellent wear resistance', developer Hadfield [15], aimed applications 'The mining industry, cement mixers, railway switches' and year 1882.
Row 2: Fe-(20-50)Mn-(3-12)Al is listed with targeted properties 'Good ductility and corrosion resistance', developer Dean and Anderson [16], application 'Electrical heating elements' and year 1943.

Row 3: Fe-34Mn-10Al-0.76C is listed with targeted properties 'Good corrosion and oxidation resistance', developer Ham and Cairns [17], application 'Replacement of Cr-Ni stainless steels' and year 1958.

Row 4: Fe-(25-30)Mn-(8-10)Al-1C is listed with targeted properties 'Precipitation hardening and good oxidation resistance', developer Kayak [18], applications 'Springs, gears, landing gears' and year 1969.
Row 5: Fe-30Mn-5Al-0.3C-Nb is listed with targeted properties 'High strength and elongation at lower temperatures', developer Kim et al. [10], application 'Cryogenic structures' and year 1985.
Row 6: Fe-(18-28)Mn-(9-12)Al-(0.7-1.2)C is listed with targeted properties 'Low weight, high crash worthiness', developer Frommeyer and Brüx [6], application 'Automotive body frames' and year 2000.
The 2000 entry (Fe-(18-28)Mn-(9-12)Al-(0.7-1.2)C) is the only row whose targeted properties combine low weight with high crash worthiness, and the only one aimed at automotive body frames.
Fe-30Mn-5Al-0.3C-Nb is the only Nb-bearing composition in the table and the only row aimed at cryogenic structures.
The caption states the table is part of a review of the 'development and applications of Fe-Mn-Al-C steels'.
The caption and abstract state that Fe-Mn-Al-C steels were previously developed in the 1950s for replacing Fe-Cr-Ni steels, consistent with the 1958 row of the table.
The superscript 'a' attached to the column header 'Alloys' indicates a footnote, but no footnote text is visible within the image.
